ostrzezenia.tekst: The internal temperature of the fish must reach 160 °F and stay there for at least 30 minutes; if your smoker cannot do this, finish cooking the fish in the oven within 2 hours of smoking. [T:MIE-071]
According to the FDA, gut any fish before salting, drying, pickling or fermenting it. [T:MIE-061]
Even vacuum-packed smoked fish must be kept in the refrigerator or freezer, never at room temperature. [T:MIE-079]

wstep: This card describes hot smoking eel at home with the method of Wisconsin Sea Grant and University of Minnesota Extension, which has been scientifically tested for safety. [T:MIE-072]

akapity: According to Wisconsin Sea Grant, any fish can be smoked, and fatty fish come out juicier than lean fish. [T:MIE-143]
Wisconsin Sea Grant does not name eel among its favorites, but says that any fish can be smoked. [T:MIE-143]
Use only high-quality fish: bad fish that goes into the smoker comes out bad. [T:MIE-143]
Hot smoking to 160 °F takes the fish above 150 °F, the temperature needed to kill parasites, so only fish for cold smoking must be frozen first. [T:MIE-078]
Cold-smoke temperatures are not hot enough to kill bacteria and may even help them grow, so this card covers hot smoking only. [T:MIE-076]
Clean freshly caught fish: gut and gill them, remove the kidney from the belly cavity, and rinse all exposed surfaces with fresh water. [T:MIE-143]
Thaw frozen fish and wash them in fresh water. [T:MIE-143]
The FDA may act against uneviscerated salt-cured, dried or smoked fish more than 5 inches long. [T:MIE-069]
Make the brine from 1 part table salt, not iodized and without anticaking agent, to 7 parts water by volume. [T:MIE-144]
1 cup of salt in 7 cups of water brines 2–3 pounds of fish; for more fish, double the amounts and keep the 1:7 ratio. [T:MIE-144]
Use a plastic or glass container, not a metal one. [T:MIE-144]
Brine in the refrigerator, at 40 °F or below (about 4 °C). [T:MIE-144]
One hour works well in many cases; you can also start with 15 minutes for each half-inch of fish thickness. [T:MIE-144]
Do not let the pieces overlap in the brine. [T:MIE-144]
Do not use recipes with longer brining in a weaker brine: they raise the chance of bacterial growth and are not recommended. [T:MIE-144]
After brining, rinse the surface of the fish. [T:MIE-144]
Place the fish skin-side down on a wire mesh screen, or hang them on hooks or dowels. [T:MIE-145]
Dry the fish with a fan until a smooth, shiny skin called a pellicle forms; on low-humidity days this usually takes 1–2 hours. [T:MIE-145]
Turn fish lying on screens from time to time. [T:MIE-145]
Insert a meat thermometer into the middle of the thickest part of the largest fish, so that it shows the lowest temperature of all the fish. [T:MIE-145]
Put a second thermometer that reads 50–250 °F (about 10–121 °C) through a hole in the smoker to watch the air temperature. [T:MIE-145]
Heat cooks and dries the fish, and smoke gives it flavor and color. [T:MIE-146]
Put the fish in when the air in the smoker reaches about 100 °F (about 38 °C). [T:MIE-146]
Your smoker must be able to reach air temperatures of 200–225 °F (about 93–107 °C). [T:MIE-146]
The internal temperature of the fish must reach 160 °F and stay there for at least 30 minutes. [T:MIE-071]
University of Idaho gives 150–160 °F for at least 30 minutes, while Wisconsin Sea Grant requires 160 °F, so this card uses 160 °F. [T:MIE-075]
With the air at 200–220 °F (about 93–104 °C) the flesh reaches about 160 °F (about 71 °C), but air temperature does not guarantee flesh temperature, so always measure the flesh. [T:MIE-146]
If your smoker cannot heat the fish enough, finish cooking it in the kitchen oven within 2 hours of smoking. [T:MIE-071]
After the fish is cooked, you can let the internal temperature drop to about 125 °F (about 52 °C) and keep smoking for flavor. [T:MIE-146]
A light smoked flavor needs about 8 hours of smoke, and smoking can take up to 12 hours. [T:MIE-146]
Use wood from oak, hickory, maple, alder, beech, apple, white birch or ash. [T:MIE-146]
Do not use pine or other resinous wood, or sawdust from fiberboard or plywood. [T:MIE-146]
Take the fish out of the smoker at once and let it cool at room temperature for about an hour. [T:MIE-146]
Then wrap it in butcher paper or cover it, and refrigerate it. [T:MIE-146]
Keep smoked fish in the refrigerator at 40 °F or below for no longer than 2 weeks, or freeze it for up to 4 months. [T:MIE-073]
Wisconsin Sea Grant allows up to a month in the refrigerator, but this card uses the shorter limit of 2 weeks from University of Idaho. [T:MIE-073,MIE-074]
Smoking does not keep fish from spoiling. [T:MIE-143]
Throw away smoked fish that has been in the refrigerator for more than 2 weeks. [T:MIE-074]
Do not keep smoked fish out of the refrigerator for more than 2 hours, or for more than 1 hour when the temperature is above 90 °F (about 32 °C). [T:SLO-408]
